how-people-use-interfaces.title: Welcome to How people actually use interfaces, part of Human-Computer Interaction.
how-people-use-interfaces.idea: Most usability problems are not caused by stupid users or lazy designers. They are caused by interfaces that assume attention, memory and patience that nobody has. A person using a mobile-money form at a market stall has one hand free, sunlight on the screen, and a queue behind them. Designing for that person produces an interface that is also easier for everybody else.
how-people-use-interfaces.example: Consider a form used to register students for a short course. Version one asks for eleven fields, requires a username and password, and validates everything at submit. In an office on a laptop, it works and looks fine. Now observe it being used where it will actually be used: a desk with a queue, a mid-range Android phone, a 3G connection, and a parent registering a child. Three problems appear immediately, and none of them are about visual taste. First: the phone keyboard for the date field opens an alphanumeric keyboard, so every date is typed by switching layouts — thousands of needless taps. Second: the password rules are invisible until submission, so the user discovers them by failing. Third: nothing is saved between attempts, so after the fourth validation error the user starts again from the top, on a connection that drops. The repair is a set of small, measurable changes: the correct keyboard type per field (inputmode="numeric" for a phone number, a date picker for the date), inline validation as the field loses focus, one clear error per field in plain language, a single primary action, optional fields postponed to a second screen, and autosave on every field so a dropped connection costs nothing. Measured again, the same task takes 90 seconds instead of four minutes, and the completion rate rises from 58% to 86% — the kind of number a form either earns or does not.
how-people-use-interfaces.challenge: Redesign one real form or flow end to end: sketch the before and after, name the principle behind each change, then test both versions with five people who did not see the design before. Report completion rate, time on task and the errors they made, and fix the worst problem your test exposed rather than the one you expected.

interaction-design-process.title: Welcome to The interaction design process, part of Human-Computer Interaction.
interaction-design-process.idea: The most expensive usability mistake is discovering a problem in code that a paper sketch would have exposed in ten minutes. Every method in this lesson exists to move learning earlier, where it is cheap: talk to six people, sketch three alternatives, test the sketch, throw it away if it fails.
interaction-design-process.example: A learning platform wants to add a certificate download. The team has one afternoon and no budget. Round 1 — paper (20 minutes per person, 5 people). Five screens drawn in a notebook. Three of the five participants looked for the certificate on the profile page, not the dashboard, because that is where they had seen the completion percentage. The flow is rearranged before a single pixel is designed. Round 2 — clickable prototype (10 minutes per person, 5 people). The button says "Download your certificate". Two participants hesitate: they are not sure the certificate is theirs yet, because the button appears while one lesson is still incomplete. The wording changes to "Certificate — finish lesson 7 to unlock", and the hesitation disappears. Round 3 — working code on the participants' own phones. Two people on 3G wait eleven seconds with no feedback and tap again, producing two downloads. A progress indicator and a disabled state fix it. Total cost: one afternoon, five participants per round, zero licences. Total value: the primary navigation for the feature changed, the wording changed, and a slow-network failure that would have generated support tickets never shipped.
interaction-design-process.challenge: Run a full formative round on a real project: three interviews or observations, one persona, one task flow, a paper or clickable prototype, five test participants, and a written findings list with severities and the change you made for each. Include the finding that surprised you, and what you had believed before the test.

accessibility-as-engineering.title: Welcome to Accessibility as engineering, part of Human-Computer Interaction.
accessibility-as-engineering.idea: The accessibility argument usually made is legal or ethical, and both are true. The engineering argument is stronger: the same changes that make an interface usable with a screen reader make it usable in sunlight, with a cracked screen, with one hand, or by somebody who is simply tired. Accessibility work is usability work with a longer list of tested conditions, and it is measurable.
accessibility-as-engineering.example: Take a course card with an image, a title, a progress bar, a price and a button. In fifteen minutes, without any paid tools: Keyboard pass. Press Tab repeatedly and note where focus goes and whether it is visible. The card's image is a link with no visible focus ring; the progress bar announces nothing; the button is a link styled as a button and works. Screen-reader pass. With a phone's built-in screen reader, the card announces "link, image, 68%, Buy now". A sighted user reads "Web Foundations, 68% complete, GH₵300". The fix is a text alternative on the image (alt="Web Foundations course cover"), an aria-label on the progress bar ("68% complete"), and a native <button> with a descriptive label. Contrast pass. The grey subtext on the light card measures 3.1:1 — below AA for body text, and only passable for large text. Darkening it to 4.6:1 fixes it without changing the design's character. Zoom pass. At 200% the price and the button overlap, because the card has a fixed height. Switching to a min-height and letting the content flow fixes it. Four fixes, none of which changed the visual design meaningfully, and the card is now usable by somebody who never uses a mouse, cannot see the difference between the greys, or reads with a screen reader. That is what accessibility work looks like in practice: unglamorous, specific and quick.
accessibility-as-engineering.challenge: Take one real screen of your own and produce an accessibility report: a keyboard pass with screenshots of focus states, a screen-reader transcript of the page, contrast measurements for every text element, a 200% zoom check, and a list of fixes with severity. Apply the fixes, then repeat the two passes and report what each change improved — and note honestly what remains unfixed and why.

mobile-first-and-low-bandwidth-design.title: Welcome to Mobile-first and low-bandwidth design, part of Human-Computer Interaction.
mobile-first-and-low-bandwidth-design.idea: In Ghana the first screen is a phone, usually mid-range Android, often shared, frequently on a prepaid data bundle that a user is consciously spending. A page that loads 6 MB to show a paragraph costs the user real money and slows down on the network they actually have. Treating those constraints as the starting point produces products that are faster for everyone, including people on fibre.
mobile-first-and-low-bandwidth-design.example: A course page loads on a mid-range Android phone over 3G. Before: 6.2 MB, 9.4 seconds to interactive, 61 requests — of which four are third-party scripts and one is an unoptimised hero image of 2.8 MB. On a 1 GB monthly bundle, opening three such pages costs about 18 MB, roughly 2% of the user's month. The repair does not require redesigning anything. Convert the hero to AVIF/WebP at the size it is displayed (2.8 MB → 92 KB), lazy-load the eight curriculum thumbnails, subset the two web fonts to Latin plus the accented characters used and self-host them (310 KB → 78 KB), replace the chat widget with a button that loads the widget on tap (220 KB deferred), and inline the critical CSS while deferring the rest. The result is 780 KB and 2.1 seconds to interactive on the same connection — a 7.9× reduction in bytes and a 4.5× improvement in time. Nothing was removed from the page; only the order and the size of what is sent changed. And the same page on a laptop with fibre now feels instant, which is the point: optimising for the worst connection improves every connection.
mobile-first-and-low-bandwidth-design.challenge: Take one page or screen of your own and put it on a data diet: a written budget, an optimisation plan, a before-and-after measurement of bytes, requests and time to interactive on a throttled real device, and a one-paragraph decision on what you refused to remove. Then have somebody on a prepaid bundle open it on their own phone and tell you what they noticed.
